MSFT.headline: Trump's threat to tax overseas data centers is only words so far, no model change
paragraphs: Nothing in the last day changes a model assumption. The one item worth understanding is President Trump's remark at a White House news conference on Friday, November 20, that the US will not allow companies to build data centers in other countries and will put a "tremendous tax" on those that do. Newsweek reports he gave no tax rate, no legal basis, no list of companies and no start date, and that he said he had not yet told his own staff.

Why it could matter: Microsoft builds data centers abroad to serve customers there, so a real tax would raise capex and cost of revenue, or slow overseas capacity and with it Intelligent Cloud revenue growth. Today it is a spoken threat with no order or bill behind it, so it is a risk to track, not a number to change. A separate Reuters exclusive from November 17 says an FCC ban on importing new models of Chinese optical transceivers, a part used inside data centers, is moving ahead. That would touch capex too, but Reuters relies on unnamed sources and gives no cost or date.

The rest of the feed is loud and old. The ByteDance briefing request is still the November 18 Reuters story, and the Nadella items come from his November 18 interviews. TechCrunch reports he defended the voluntary buyout offered in October to about 60,000 employees, with no terms, uptake or cost disclosed, so there is nothing yet to put through operating margin.
watch: Any written order, bill or tax rate following Trump's overseas data center remark, and whether Microsoft's foreign projects are named
A formal FCC step on Chinese optical transceivers, and any estimate of what replacing them costs
Buyout uptake and any one time charge, which would show up in operating margin
MSFT.note: Confirmed by Microsoft: nothing new; it declined to comment to both Newsweek and Reuters. Reported only: Trump's remarks and their lack of detail (Newsweek, read on Yahoo; the CNBC and Washington Times articles could not be opened), the transceiver ban (Reuters, unnamed sources, read on Yahoo Finance), and Nadella's buyout comments (TechCrunch); CNBC's Nadella piece on cyber defenses is headline only, article not read.
